evidence.title: Diffusion of responsibility: Patient moral judgments of generative AI-informed clinical decisions
evidence.outcome: Patient moral blame of physician after adverse outcome, by adherence to GAI advice
evidence.effect: Physicians who adhered to GAI advice incurred significantly less moral blame than those who did not (p < 0.001). The effect was stronger for personalized regimens (p < 0.001) than for standard-of-care (p < 0.05).
evidence.quote: The analysis shows a significant diffusion of responsibility i.e., when an adverse outcome occurs, physicians who adhere to GAI advice incur significantly less moral blame than those who do not (p < 0.001).

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether defining and recording accountability for AI errors among clinicians, institutions, and developers reduces harm or clarifies recourse. Eight hazard studies report that clinicians and other stakeholders perceive accountability as unresolved, and the recommendation rests on those studies and 89 endorsing sources.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Eight hazard studies, mostly qualitative or small surveys, consistently report unclear accountability. They show that the problem exists. They cannot show whether documented accountability arrangements change liability outcomes, clinician behavior, or patient recourse.

Among 25 oncologists, 88% (70.0-95.8) expected to bear primary legal responsibility for AI errors. In 484 Reddit comments, clinicians described their signature as a legal shock absorber for institutional AI liability. If blame defaults to the signing clinician, model or institutional failures may go unreported to developers. No study tests whether documented accountability changes this.

In a deployed prescribing tool, 13 endocrinologists named accountability and liability among the themes that hindered adoption. In a UK study of 40 participants, clinicians felt ultimately liable while relying on AI-generated insights. These findings suggest that unresolved accountability may affect uptake. No study measured the burden or fidelity of documenting accountability in practice.

In a vignette study of 331 participants, physicians who followed generative AI advice drew less moral blame after an adverse outcome than those who did not (p < 0.001). This suggests that patients may shift fault toward the AI, which could complicate recourse. In a US focus group that included patient advocates, participants split on whether providers should bear full responsibility.

Of 25 physicians in Luxembourg, 64% (44.5-79.8) cited regulatory or legal uncertainty as a barrier. In a separate survey of 18 clinicians, 92% reported uncertainty about legal protection. Endorsing sources differ on how to allocate liability, and one assigns it to developers of autonomous systems. No study examines whether institutional accountability records affect liability determinations.

None of the eight hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One interview study included stakeholders in Nigeria but did not enroll patients. The evidence therefore cannot indicate how accountability gaps affect patients who have fewer means to pursue recourse after harm.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems or deployments with and without documented accountability arrangements for AI. Such a study would need to measure error reporting to developers, time to resolution of AI-related incidents, clinician adoption, patient complaints and recourse, and legal outcomes. Studies would also need to record how liability is divided in vendor contracts and whether those terms match what clinicians believe.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and none of the hazard studies reports enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Most participants were clinicians, developers, or administrators rather than patients. The evidence therefore cannot indicate whether accountability arrangements would help patients who face language, literacy, or financial barriers to complaint and legal recourse.
